title: XI-XXI: distinctions of divine science
pass_a_gloss: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): a science distinct out from simple intelligence plus vision does not seem needed. but make it a part belonging toward simple intelligence; — i do not deny ye thing itself belonging toward middle science. These plus like distinctions stand as taken out from our mode belonging toward knowing. XXI. It stands as theoretical or practical. XVIII–XX. free that same by means belonging toward that same which God after ye free act belonging toward His will distinctly understands all future things. It stands as natural or free — natural nearly ye same as simple intelligence; XV–XVII. after ye decree belonging toward will, knows besides Himself all other things that same which are, will be, or have been — science belonging toward vision stands as that same by means belonging toward that same which God. XIV. preceding in God ye free act belonging toward will — science belonging toward simple intelligence stands as ye cognition belonging toward all possibles. XIII. in that same which they consider a middle science before free will's decrees — some set a fourth instant after ye first. in ye third, science belonging toward vision. in ye second, decrees belonging toward free will; In ye first instant belonging toward reason they place science belonging toward simple intelligence; It stands as science belonging toward simple intelligence or belonging toward vision. XII. that same which in itself stands as unique plus most simple, according to various objects plus respects to objects — but in species ye schools distinguish God's science. XI.
pass_b_english: XI. But in species the schools distinguish God's science, which in itself is unique and most simple, according to various objects and respects to objects. XII. It is science of simple intelligence or of vision. In the first instant of reason they place science of simple intelligence; in the second, decrees of free will; in the third, science of vision. Some set a fourth instant after the first, in which they consider a middle science before free will's decrees.

XIII. Science of simple intelligence is the cognition of all possibles, preceding in God the free act of will. XIV. Science of vision is that by which God, after the decree of will, knows besides Himself all other things which are, will be, or have been. XV–XVII. It is natural or free — natural nearly the same as simple intelligence; free that by which God after the free act of His will distinctly understands all future things. XVIII–XX. It is theoretical or practical. XXI. These and like distinctions are taken from our mode of knowing. I do not deny the thing itself of middle science, but make it a part of simple intelligence; a science distinct from simple intelligence and vision does not seem needed.
source_text: XI. In specie vero scientiam Dei, quae quidem per se unica et simplicissima est, scholae distinguunt secundum varia objecta et respectus ad objecta. XII. Est scientia simplicis intelligentiae aut visionis. In primo instanti rationis scientiam simplicis intelligentiae; in altero liberae voluntatis decreta; in tertio scientiam visionis collocant. Quidam quartum instans post primum constituunt, in quo scientiam mediam considerant ante libera voluntatis decreta. XIII. Scientia simplicis intelligentiae est cognitio omnium possibilium, in Deo liberum actum voluntatis antecedens. XIV. Scientia visionis est qua Deus cognoscit praeter se post decretum voluntatis omnia alia quae sunt, erunt aut fuerunt. XV-XVII. Est naturalis aut libera — naturalis eadem fere cum simplici intelligentia; libera qua Deus post liberum actum voluntatis omnes res futuras distincte intelligit. XVIII-XX. Est theoretica aut practica. XXI. Hae aliaeque similes distinctiones sumuntur e nostro cognoscendi modo. Rem ipsam scientiae mediae non nego, sed partem facio simplicis intelligentiae; distincta scientia a simplici intelligentia et visione non videtur opus esse.
